source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Two-stage retrieval. MAC is a cheap, structure-blind dot product of content vectors over all memory. FAC runs full structure mapping (SME) on the few items MAC passes. Aim: explain why retrieval is surface-driven yet rare analogical remindings still occur.
numbers: MAC selector returns best score plus everything within 10% of it; FAC selector same 10% width. Content vector = count of each predicate (functor) in a description.
limits: Paper header says 1994 but the true year is 1995. Memory in the simulations is tiny (18 to 36 stories).
agent_relevance: Direct blueprint for a memory step: cheap index over all items, then an expensive structural check on a handful.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Content vectors: one slot per predicate type, value = how many times it occurs in the description. The dot product of two vectors estimates how many match hypotheses SME would build. It usually overestimates (ignores argument alignment) and can underestimate (ignores non-identical functions).
numbers: Normalised variant divides by counts; binary variant records only presence. Cost about 0.002 s per vector pair in 1990s Lisp.
limits: Dot product ignores structure by design; it only scores, gives no correspondences or inferences.
agent_relevance: A count vector of relation types (as SUBFIELDS.md proposes) is a legitimate cheap first pass; it is cheap to compute from LLM-written relation lists.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Design criteria the model must meet: surface superiority in retrieval, primacy of mundane (literal) matches, rare insights (analogies must sometimes surface), scalability, and structural soundness of what is returned.
numbers: Five criteria stated in section 2; MAC provides most filtering, FAC supplies soundness and candidate inferences.
limits: Criteria are the authors' own, fitted to the Karla data.
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist to test any agent memory: does it retrieve analogies at least sometimes without flooding with junk.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Human target data (Rattermann & Gentner 1987 Exp 2, cited in the paper): subjects memorised 32 stories (20 base, 12 distractors), a week later read 20 probes and wrote down remindings. Retrieval order was literal similarity = surface > analogy = first-order only; soundness ratings were the reverse (analogy and literal most sound).
numbers: Proportion reminded: LS .56, SF .53, AN .12, FOR .09. 5 probes per type. LS and SF not significantly different.
limits: Reported here as cited summary inside the MAC/FAC paper, not re-run. In Exp 2 AN and FOR did not differ; in Exp 1 AN beat FOR.
agent_relevance: Humans retrieve what looks alike, not what is structurally alike, and still prefer structural matches once both are in view. Retrieval and judgement are different filters.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Simulation 1: memory holds 9 base stories plus 9 FOR distractors; probes are LS, SF, AN variants. Base story retrieved by both MAC and FAC.
numbers: Correct retrieval: LS 1.0, SF 0.89, AN 0.67 (MAC and FAC identical). Order LS > SF > AN matches humans, but accuracy is far above human rates.
limits: Memory 18 stories vs 32 for humans; no delay or forgetting; the authors admit the task is easier than the human one.
agent_relevance: Analogical retrieval works at 2/3 hit rate on a tiny clean memory; do not expect that on a large noisy one.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Simulation 2 (harder): all four variants of 9 story sets in memory (36 stories), base used as probe. Mean matches retrieved per probe through MAC then FAC. FAC acts as a structural filter: it keeps all LS hits, some SF and AN, and rejects most FOR and other-set items.
numbers: MAC passes mean 3.4 items, FAC keeps mean 1.6. LS 0.78 and 0.78. Wrong-set items: MAC 1.33, FAC 0.22. Order LS > SF > AN > FOR.
limits: Table text is OCR-damaged; only the LS values, the 3.4/1.6 means and the wrong-set figures are certain.
agent_relevance: The second stage cut wrong-set junk from 1.33 to 0.22 per probe: the value of FAC is junk rejection.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Simulation 3: remove literal-similarity items from memory. Surface matches then win, then analogies, then first-order-only, matching the human ordering SF > AN > FOR.
numbers: Mean retrieved per probe, MAC/FAC: SF 0.88/0.78, FOR 0.56/0.56, other 1.11/0.11 (AN row damaged in extraction). 27 stories in memory.
limits: Ordinal fit only; exact percentages not matched by design.
agent_relevance: With no good literal match around, surface lookalikes still crowd out real analogues; expect the same from an embedding index.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Sensitivity analysis of selector widths. Data fit only when MAC width is 10 to 20 percent and FAC width at least 10 percent. MAC 1 percent or FAC 1 percent: analogies never retrieved. MAC 30 percent or more with wide FAC: first too many analogies, then junk.
numbers: Grid of 11 x 11 widths (1 to 100 percent); viable zone for original content vectors is MAC 10-20 percent. Unnormalised vectors shift it to MAC 30-50 percent; binary vectors similar.
limits: Run on the 9 encoded Karla sets only. Normalisation details did not matter, selector width did.
agent_relevance: The cut-off after the cheap stage is the key tuning knob: too narrow kills far analogues, too wide floods the expensive step. Tune it on held-out probes.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Ablation of what goes in the content vector. Attribute-only vectors cannot satisfy the data; relation-only vectors also fail (more junk when MAC above 40 percent or FAC above 70 percent). The mix of attributes, relations and logical connectives is needed.
numbers: Tables 9 and 10 of the paper; no single viable region comparable to Table 6 for either ablation.
limits: Small simulated corpus.
agent_relevance: Do not index on surface words alone nor on relations alone; the cheap vector needs both.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: MAC/FAC versus ARCS (Thagard et al 1990 retrieval model, WordNet-based, constraint network). Probing the Karla base story in a Fables (100) plus Plays (25) memory, MAC/FAC always finds the base story for every variant probe; ARCS ranks it low (negative activations in places) and its order was LS, FOR, appearance, analogy, unlike humans.
numbers: MAC/FAC run times 6 to 37 s versus ARCS 17 to 614 s per probe; roughly two orders of magnitude faster. Some Section 4 encodings would not settle in ARCS even after 1000 iterations (12 h runs).
limits: Authors are the rival modellers; ARCS was run on translated encodings. Results on 1 to 3 hand-built story sets.
agent_relevance: Cheap-filter-first beats a global constraint-satisfaction retrieval on speed and fit.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Hamlet and West Side Story probes against Shakespeare plays: for West Side Story, FAC scores Romeo and Juliet 16.51 (near-isomorphic) so only it survives; for Hamlet FAC is indifferent, scores 6.79 vs 5.49 vs 3.72 vs 2.67, drop-off 20 percent which is under the 100 percent default cutoff, so several plays return.
numbers: MAC scores for West Side Story: Othello .86, Macbeth .85, Romeo and Juliet .83.
limits: Two probes, hand-encoded plays.
agent_relevance: FAC's score gap, not an absolute threshold, decides whether one or many analogues come back; useful to decide how many retrieved cases to show.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Stated limitations. Retrieval failure only possible if FAC rejects all of MAC's candidates. False negatives are argued to be cheaper than false positives because retrieval is iterative: reformulating or re-representing the probe can catch a missed item. Scaling issue: content vector size grows with vocabulary.
numbers: Claimed speed edge over ARCS about two orders of magnitude. Also tested on 30 metaphors (about 12 propositions each), 12 physical descriptions (about 42), and Karla set (45 descriptions, about 67 propositions each).
limits: Authors claim consistent, but these extra data sets are not reported in detail.
agent_relevance: Supports retry-with-reformulated-probe loops for memory access rather than one-shot retrieval.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: Analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events, Cognitive Science 33:1343-1382
finding: Experiment 1 (management consultants, negotiation classes). Two analogous negotiation cases read side by side and compared (comparison group) vs analysed separately. Comparing at recall time raised retrieval of a relationally matching example from the person's own life memory, and also use of the principle in a role-play negotiation.
numbers: Retrieval-quality rating: comparison M=1.25 vs separate M=0.82, t(122)=2.65, p<.01. Linked the two cases: 88% vs 17%. Contingent agreements in test negotiation: 59% vs 33%, chi2(1,N=62)=4.22, p<.05. Among all recalled items: 52% analogies, 6% literal, 30% shallow, 11% other.
limits: Self-report autobiographical memory; coded by blind raters, truth of recalled events not checkable (66% of examples were own or colleagues' experience).
agent_relevance: Showing the model two analogous cases and asking for the common schema, then using the schema as the probe, retrieves far analogues much better than a single case does.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: Analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events, Cognitive Science 33:1343-1382
finding: Experiment 2 with Masters of Accounting students replicated Experiment 1: comparing two cases improved articulation of the principle and retrieval from own memory.
numbers: N=36. Principle quality M=1.42 vs 0.53, t(34)=3.41, p<.01. Retrieval ratings 1.47 vs 0.59, t(34)=2.88, p<.01. Principle and retrieval correlated rs=.51. Linked cases 95% vs 18%. 86% retrieved some example; only 35% were business situations.
limits: Small N; same materials and scorer as Exp 1.
agent_relevance: The effect holds in a second population with the same procedure.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: Analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events, Cognitive Science 33:1343-1382
finding: Experiment 3 extended to two principle types (contingent contracts and trade-offs) with a single-case control as well as a separate-case control. Comparison beat both controls on principle articulation and on relational retrieval; for trade-offs articulation the gap was not significant.
numbers: Retrieval: comparison M=1.08 vs controls, F(.,48)=10.38 (first df lost in extraction), MSE=0.38, p<.005; Dunnett p<.05 against both controls. Principle quality overall comparison M=1.33, F(1,48)=8.63, p<.01. Trade-off articulation 1.17 vs 0.78 n.s. (t(46)=1.66, p=.10). Linking cases: 100% vs 36%.
limits: About 50 participants total; retrieval from natural memory is hard to verify.
agent_relevance: The benefit needs the comparison itself, not just seeing two cases or seeing one.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: Analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events, Cognitive Science 33:1343-1382
finding: Experiment 4 with a controlled memory set. Seven negotiation cases learned, 30 minutes of filler, then two analogous probe cases. Comparing the two probes lifted retrieval of the stored analogue about fourfold and cut retrieval of a surface-similar case.
numbers: N=73 (37 comparison, 36 separate). Analogous example recalled: 27% vs 6%, chi2(1,N=73)=6.12, p<.05. Surface-similar example recalled: 30% vs 78%.
limits: Absolute analogue retrieval is still low (27%) even in the best condition; one analogue among seven stored cases.
agent_relevance: Even in the best case far-analogue retrieval is a minority outcome; plan for most probes to return nothing relational.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: Analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events, Cognitive Science 33:1343-1382
finding: Experiment 5: comparing two current problems before solving them raised transfer from a single stored analogy (Gick and Holyoak fortress story, 25 min earlier, filled delay) to the tumor-radiation problem. Explicit reminding was rare in both groups.
numbers: N=227 (116 vs 111). Tumor convergence solution 31% vs 5%, chi2(1,N=227)=24.71, p<.001. Red Adair problem 41% vs 30%, p=.08 n.s. Reminded of earlier story: 18% vs 14%. Of 21 comparison participants who recalled it, 81% solved vs 33% (n=95) who did not. Kurtz & Loewenstein 2007 (cited): about 50% vs 15%.
limits: Red Adair effect not significant; the authors cannot explain why the control did well there (familiar domain).
agent_relevance: Writing a schema from two current subproblems may make stored solutions accessible without any explicit retrieval step.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: Analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events, Cognitive Science 33:1343-1382
finding: Simulations 1-4 with MAC/FAC (MAC and FAC each return up to 3 items) over a memory of 76 stories. An SME-built relational schema (about 80% relational predicates vs about 40% in a base story) used as probe retrieves analogies; a concrete story probe mostly retrieves shallow surface matches.
numbers: Sim 1 FAC: base stories retrieved shallow matches 86% and 100%, analogies 14% and 0%; schema probe retrieved analogies 86%, shallow 29%, first-order-only 14%. Sim 2 (literal matches present): story probe retrieved literal matches 100% and no analogies; schema probe gave literal 71% and analogy 86%, shallow 14%.
limits: Hand-encoded story sets, seven items per type; the schema is built by SME from known analogues, so the sim shows the effect given a good schema.
agent_relevance: Direct computational support for the idea that probe abstraction, not a better index, fixes far-analogue retrieval.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: Analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events, Cognitive Science 33:1343-1382
finding: The introduction surveys why transfer fails: remindings follow surface similarity (Gick & Holyoak 1980, 1983; Ross 1984, 1987, 1989; Brooks 1987; Catrambone 2002; Gentner et al. 1993). Experts do better than novices (Blanchette & Dunbar 2001; Novick 1988). Comparing analogous examples at learning is the best-established way to promote relational transfer (Gick & Holyoak 1983; Catrambone & Holyoak 1989; Ross & Kennedy 1990; Gentner et al. 2003).
numbers: No new numbers; statement of the literature.
limits: Secondary summary by authors with a stake in comparison theory.
agent_relevance: Gives the list of core experiments to chase backward: Gick-Holyoak, Ross, Catrambone-Holyoak, Novick.

source: Gentner & Forbus (1991) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Proc. 13th Cognitive Science Society
finding: First published form of MAC/FAC. Cites Rattermann & Gentner 1987: subjects read a large story set and were tested two weeks later; retrieval proportions LS .56, SF .53, AN .12, FOR .09 (same as in the 1995 paper). Early simulation already gives order LS > SF > AN > FOR.
numbers: Same 10% selector width for MAC and FAC; early simulation tables use the same story sets (details not extracted).
limits: Paper text says two weeks' delay; the 1995 paper says about a week, so the delay differs between accounts.
agent_relevance: Shows the model was fixed in 1991 and the 1995 work is sensitivity analysis and the ARCS comparison, not a new model.

source: Law, Forbus & Gentner (1994) Simulating similarity-based retrieval: A comparison of ARCS and MAC/FAC, Proc. 16th Cognitive Science Society, 543-548
finding: Head-to-head test of MAC/FAC and the Thagard et al. (1990) ARCS retrieval model on the ARCS authors' own encodings (100 fables, 25 plays, Karla, Sour Grapes, Hamlet, West Side Story). MAC/FAC was about two orders of magnitude faster, and its results were stable when plays were added to a fables memory while ARCS's results changed.
numbers: Run times per probe: MAC/FAC about 0.2 to 37 s, ARCS about 17 to 614 s. ARCS hinted at a size bias (prefers larger stories). Increasing memory by 25% changed ARCS answers. Karla base story found by MAC/FAC for every variant probe.
limits: Same authors as the model; few probes; ARCS needed a definition of what counts as a retrieval that its authors never gave.
agent_relevance: Retrieval results should be tested for stability when the pool of distractors changes; a score that shifts with memory size is a warning sign.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC (section 2 literature review)
finding: Founding dissociation (Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus 1993, as summarised): surface similarity best predicts which memory comes to mind; structural similarity best predicts rated soundness. It held between subjects and within subjects: people judged the very matches that came to mind most easily (surface matches) to be unsound.
numbers: Retrieval order LS > SF > AN > FOR; soundness order AN, LS above SF, FOR. Higher-order relations added to a probe gave non-significantly more retrieval in two studies and a small significant gain in the third.
limits: Second-hand summary; the 1993 PDF is a scan and could not be text-extracted in this session.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the first thing retrieved: judge retrieved cases with a separate structural-soundness check.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC (section 2 literature review)
finding: Gick and Holyoak (1980, 1983) inert-analogy result as cited: subjects given the fortress story then the radiation problem solved it about 30 percent of the time; when told to use the story, 80 to 90 percent solved. So the story was in memory but not spontaneously accessed.
numbers: About 30% spontaneous vs 80-90% when hinted.
limits: Numbers are rounded in the MAC/FAC paper; the 1980 original was not opened. The Gentner 2009 paper cites a 15% rate for no-hint tumor-problem solving in later work.
agent_relevance: The failure is retrieval, not mapping: a hint or a probe rewrite that points at the right stored item fixes it.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC (section 2 literature review)
finding: Boundary conditions named in the paper: higher-order relational matches raise retrieval when encoding of the original is intensive (Faries & Reiser 1988) or when subjects are experts (Novick 1988a,b). Indexed case-based reasoning models (Schank, Kolodner) wrongly predict that the best structural match is typically retrieved and have no corpus of 10^3 to 10^6 structured cases to show scalability.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Argument from authors defending a feature-vector first stage.
agent_relevance: Deliberate rewriting of stored memories into abstract terms (intensive encoding) is the lever that makes relational retrieval work; an expert-written index can do the same.

source: Raynal, Clement, Gros & Sander (2026) Bridging the retrieval gap: Familiar schema-governed categories support reminding of disparate events, Memory & Cognition 54:1965-1980
finding: Experiment 1 replicates the classic pattern with everyday-life memories: when the cue shares both surface and structure with memories, close analogues beat distant (structure-only) analogues.
numbers: N=133. Close analogues M=0.47 (SD .57) vs distant M=0.09 (SD .31), t(132)=14.45, p<.001, d=0.84. 502 memories reported; 85.7% had surface overlap, 63.6% had surface plus full structure, 11.8% structure only.
limits: University students; self-reported memories coded by raters; cue sentences preserve the usual surface/structure pairing.
agent_relevance: Surface-dominant retrieval is robust in new data three decades on.

source: Raynal, Clement, Gros & Sander (2026) Bridging the retrieval gap: Familiar schema-governed categories support reminding of disparate events, Memory & Cognition 54:1965-1980
finding: Experiment 2 breaks the classic result: when cues pair familiar structures with unusual surfaces (so surface matches and structural matches compete directly), people retrieve distant analogues far more than surface-only matches.
numbers: N=81. Distant analogues M=0.46 (SD .68) vs surface matches M=0.04 (SD .20), t(80)=12.06, p<.001, d=0.82. 311 memories; 83.6% had no surface overlap, 66.8% structure only. Usual surface/structure combos were retrieved more (M=0.25 vs 0.06, t(80)=7.86).
limits: Structure here is a familiar Schema-Governed Category (making up an excuse, pretending to like a gift). Unfamiliar structures were not tested here. Retrievals still favoured usual surface/structure pairings.
agent_relevance: Relational retrieval works when the structure is a well-known named category; naming the pattern is the lever.

source: Raynal, Clement, Gros & Sander (2026) Bridging the retrieval gap: Familiar schema-governed categories support reminding of disparate events, Memory & Cognition 54:1965-1980
finding: Experiment 3 (cues stripped of all surface features) elicited more retrievals of usual than unusual surface/structure combinations, suggesting association frequency influences analogical retrieval. The authors argue classical two-phase lab designs underestimate non-experts because lab stimuli are encoded shallowly.
numbers: N=95 (df 94). 411 memories, 82.24% full structural match, 17.27% partial, 0.49% none. Usual surface/structure combos M=0.26 (SD .45) vs unusual M=0.01 (SD .10), t(94)=11.82, p<.001, d=0.54. Usual combos were retrieved less than in Exp 1 when cues lost surface features (0.47 in Exp 1), t(226)=-6.90, d=-0.40.
limits: Exploratory comparison across experiments, not randomised.
agent_relevance: Stored memories tagged with a familiar abstract category label may be reachable by far probes.

source: Raynal, Clement & Sander (2025) The role of surface and structural similarities in the retrieval of realistic perceptual events, British Journal of Psychology
finding: Video-clip paradigm: after watching clips, a new cue clip shared surface features with one earlier clip and abstract structure (once bitten twice shy etc.) with another. Structure beat surface in Experiment 1A and 2, the reverse of the classic text-based finding.
numbers: Exp 1A: of 113 single-source participants, 71.68% retrieved the structure-only analogue, 18.58% the surface-only lookalike, 9.74% a neutral clip; chi2(1, N=101) significant. Exp 2 (larger set of unrelated clips): 82.41% vs 10.19% vs 7.41%, chi2(1, N=99)=60.83, p<.001, phi=.78.
limits: Only a small set (six initial clips); familiar everyday structures; participants asked to indicate a reminding. Authors say reactivation-mapping serial comparison cannot be ruled out in 1A.
agent_relevance: With a small, shallowly different memory, structure can win; scale up distractors (Exp 2) and it still held here.

source: Raynal, Clement & Sander (2025) The role of surface and structural similarities in the retrieval of realistic perceptual events, British Journal of Psychology
finding: Control Experiment 1B removes the structural competitor and shows the surface cues were strong: when only a surface lookalike was available, nearly everyone retrieved it.
numbers: 42 single-source participants: 88.10% surface lookalike, 7.14% surface-different clip without structural overlap, 4.76% other; chi2(1,N=39)=28.9, p<.001, phi=.86.
limits: Same small clip set.
agent_relevance: Surface power and structural power are both real; which wins depends on competition and familiarity of the structure.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur & Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining, KDD (arXiv 1706.05585)
finding: Cheap learned structural proxy for retrieval over large messy text. Crowd workers labelled about 8000 product descriptions for purpose and mechanism; an RNN learned purpose and mechanism vectors. Pairs ranked by these vectors give higher precision than TF-IDF, LSA, LDA or GloVe baselines.
numbers: Test set 2500 pairs, training about 5500 products. Precision at top 1%: purpose-only 0.739, mechanism-only 0.696, TF-IDF 0.630, LSA 0.413, LDA 0.435. At top 5%: purpose-only 0.612 vs TF-IDF 0.463.
limits: Labels are noisy; negatives were implicit (rejected top-5 results, not true negatives); some positives were surface-only. Small domain (product descriptions).
agent_relevance: A learned two-field index (purpose, mechanism) is a practical middle ground between SME and keyword search for stored cases.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur & Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining, KDD (arXiv 1706.05585)
finding: Ideation experiment: analogies retrieved by the learned model (similar purpose cluster, diverse mechanism) were given as inspirations when redesigning products; participants produced more good ideas than with TF-IDF or random inspirations.
numbers: 749 ideas collected. On the 9 seeds in all three conditions: good ideas 46% (N=105) analogy model vs 37% random (49) vs 30% TF-IDF (54), p<=.01 (2-proportion). Majority-vote threshold k=3: 38% vs 22% random vs 21% TF-IDF. Logistic model: B=-1.81 (vs TF-IDF) and -1.88 (vs random), p<.01 at k=2.
limits: Wide confidence intervals; one task type; crowd judges; authors call for replication.
agent_relevance: Retrieved analogies helped only when they were structural; TF-IDF retrievals did no better than random.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer & Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives, arXiv 2310.00996
finding: Benchmark of 548 narrative pairs built from proverb narratives, split into near (same domain) and far (cross-domain) analogies with near or far distractors. Zero-shot LLMs recognise near analogies but fail far ones; GPT-4 scored below chance on far analogies.
numbers: Mean accuracy over tested LLMs (random 50%): near analogy vs far distractor 76.9, near vs near 73.2, far vs far 45.3, far analogy vs near distractor 33.9; overall 57.3. Humans 98.6, 97.2, 96.8, 91.4; overall 96.0. Near analogies: models 75.0 vs humans 97.9; far analogies: models 39.6 vs humans 94.1. SBERT similarity alone 77.9 on near.
limits: This is a pair-choice task, not retrieval from a store; models were tested zero-shot and with few-shot demonstrations (gain not reproduced in full here).
agent_relevance: LLMs show the human surface bias in extreme form: a surface-similar distractor beats a deeper analogue. Retrieval by plain semantic similarity will return lookalikes.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR (arXiv 2310.01714)
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own relevant example problems then solves the target. It beats 0-shot CoT and fixed few-shot CoT without needing a retrieval store.
numbers: GSM8K rows read in order 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, 5-shot CoT, ours: GPT-3.5-turbo 75.0, 75.8, 76.7, 77.8; text-davinci-003 14.8, 50.3, 54.0, 61.0; PaLM2 60.8, 78.2, 80.7, 81.7. MATH GPT-3.5: 33.0, 33.9, 34.9, 37.3. Codeforces Acc@1 best variant 15% (GPT-3.5-16k) and 19% (GPT-4). Reported average gain about +4%.
limits: Table text extracted from PDF with row labels partly lost; row order is inferred. Self-generated examples can be wrong.
agent_relevance: Cheap alternative to MAC/FAC: generate rather than retrieve. Check numbers against the table in the paper before quoting.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR (arXiv 2310.01714)
finding: Generate versus retrieve: self-generated exemplars beat retrieved exemplars (cosine similarity of train set) only for larger models; smaller models do better with retrieved labelled exemplars.
numbers: GSM8K by model scale: text-curie-001 2% for fixed and retrieved CoT; text-davinci-003 5-shot fixed CoT 50%, 5-shot retrieved CoT 54%, self-generated 61% (last value inferred from the garbled table). Self-generation fails to produce valid exemplars on small models.
limits: Retrieval baseline is plain embedding similarity, not an analogical retriever; GSM8K train and test are same distribution.
agent_relevance: Own-memory generation depends on the model already having related knowledge; a weaker agent needs real retrieval from a store.

source: Larraz & Corma (2026) Human analogical guidance amplifies LLM performance through cross-domain knowledge activation, Nature Communications
finding: Qwen-2.5-7B with retrieval-augmented generation restricted to pre-1936 literature was asked to design a fluid catalytic cracker. The needed cross-domain precedents (grain silo flows, Stokes law) were in the retrieved context, but unguided runs never used them. A human analogical hint made the model use them.
numbers: Baseline 2/20 successes (10%, CI 1-32%); grain-silo analogy guidance 20/20 (100%, CI 83-100%), p<0.001. Stokes law used 0/20 baseline vs 18/20 scaffolded; heat-management concepts used 18/20 baseline vs 1/20 scaffolded.
limits: One historical case, one 7B model, 250 trials in all, the two baseline successes may be pretraining leakage; steering parts not relevant here.
agent_relevance: Putting a far analogue into context is not enough; the agent needs an explicit step that says which stored analogue to map. Matches the human retrieval gap but at the use stage.
